# A First Report, by Hand {#sec-first-report}

```{python}
#| label: first-setup
import csv
import difflib
import fnmatch
import hashlib
import re
from pathlib import Path

from IPython.display import Markdown

from scripts.prose import number_words, text_holds

# The starter readers copy in this chapter (cells run from book/). Every number in the prose
# is read from its data file, and the one typed figure from its report.qmd.
START = Path("../starters/first-report")
CSV = START / "data" / "visits.csv"
csv_text = CSV.read_text()
with open(CSV, newline="") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
visits = {r["attraction"]: int(r["visits_2025"]) for r in rows}
WORD = number_words()
n_rows, n_cols = WORD[len(rows)], WORD[len(rows[0])]
total = sum(visits.values())
top = max(visits, key=visits.get)
n_free = sum(r["admission"].startswith("Free") for r in rows)
tate = visits["Tate Modern"]
# What `ls` lists in a fresh copy: the starter's files, less what .gitignore leaves out (a
# local test render of the starter would otherwise add report.html).
ignore = [l.strip("/") for l in (START / ".gitignore").read_text().split()]


def kept(p: Path) -> bool:
    """Whether Git records this path: no part of it matches a .gitignore pattern."""
    return not any(fnmatch.fnmatch(part, pat) for part in p.relative_to(START).parts for pat in ignore)


names = {p.name for p in START.iterdir() if not p.name.startswith(".") and kept(p)}
text_holds(names == {"report.qmd", "data", "AGENTS.md", "README.md", "pyproject.toml", "uv.lock"},
           "the table of the starter's files")
n_files = WORD[len(names)]
# The first commit's summary in the transcript: the files Git records and their lines.
tracked = [p for p in START.rglob("*") if p.is_file() and kept(p)]
text_holds((len(tracked), sum(len(p.read_text().splitlines()) for p in tracked)) == (7, 916),
           "the first commit's 7 files changed, 916 insertions(+)")


def code(value) -> Markdown:
    """A value set as code in a sentence, for something the reader types or reads on screen."""
    return Markdown(f"`{value}`")


# The planted mistake: the one figure typed into the report's prose.
report = (START / "report.qmd").read_text()
typed = re.search(r"Tate Modern, on the South Bank, had ([0-9,]+) visits\.", report)
text_holds(typed is not None, "the starter's typed sentence about Tate Modern")
planted = int(typed.group(1).replace(",", ""))
a, b = str(planted), str(tate)
diff_at = [i for i in range(len(a)) if a[i] != b[i]] if len(a) == len(b) else []
# The prose says two neighbouring digits are swapped.
text_holds(len(diff_at) == 2 and diff_at[1] == diff_at[0] + 1
           and (a[diff_at[0]], a[diff_at[1]]) == (b[diff_at[1]], b[diff_at[0]]),
           "the planted figure (two neighbouring digits swapped)")
gap = abs(tate - planted)
# The prose says it is the only typed number: outside the front matter, the cell and the
# inline code, the report's text holds no figures but the year and the planted one.
body = report.split("---", 2)[2]
body = re.sub(r"```\{python\}.*?```", "", body, flags=re.S)
body = re.sub(r"`\{python\}[^`]*`", "", body)
text_holds(set(re.findall(r"[0-9][0-9,]*", body)) == {"2025", typed.group(1)},
           "the report's only typed number")
# Its four values (a total, a name, a count and the free count) are inline code.
text_holds(len(re.findall(r"(?<!`)`\{python\}", report)) == 4, "the report's four pieces of inline code")

# The reader's trial edit: Tate Modern's first digit, raised by one.
BUMP = 10 ** (len(b) - 1)
trial = tate + BUMP
text_holds(str(trial)[1:] == b[1:] and len(str(trial)) == len(b), "the first-digit edit")
# The prediction: the most visited and the free count stay; the total rises by BUMP.
text_holds(top != "Tate Modern" and trial < visits[top], "the unchanged most visited sight")
total_after = total + BUMP
first_old, first_new = b[0], str(trial)[0]
# nano opens on the header line: the down arrow reaches the Tate Modern row this many times.
csv_lines = csv_text.splitlines()
downs = WORD[next(i for i, line in enumerate(csv_lines) if line.startswith("Tate Modern,"))]
# `cut -d,` splits at every comma, so the prose's two-column view is right only while the
# first two columns hold none.
text_holds(all("," not in r["attraction"] for r in rows), "the cut command's safe columns")


def screen(lines: list[str]) -> None:
    """Print lines as a terminal screen (the cell is `output: asis`, inside ::: transcript),
    in a fence longer than any run of backticks inside them."""
    ticks = "`" * max(3, 1 + max((len(m) for l in lines for m in re.findall("`+", l)), default=0))
    print(f"{ticks}text\n" + "\n".join(lines) + f"\n{ticks}")


def git_hunks(old: list[str], new: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """The hunks `git diff` prints: difflib's, with Git's default context after each `@@`
    (the last line above the hunk that starts with a letter, `_` or `$`)."""
    out = []
    for line in list(difflib.unified_diff(old, new, lineterm=""))[2:]:
        if line.startswith("@@"):
            start = int(re.match(r"@@ -(\d+)", line).group(1))
            above = (l for l in reversed(old[:start - 1]) if re.match(r"[A-Za-z_$]", l))
            line = f"{line} {next(above, '')}".rstrip()
        out.append(line)
    return out


def short(line: str, width: int = 40) -> str:
    """Cut a long line for a phone's width, marking the cut with an ellipsis."""
    return line if len(line) <= width else line[:width] + "…"


def blob(text: str) -> str:
    """Git's short name for a file's contents (its blob hash), as `git diff` prints it."""
    data = text.encode()
    return hashlib.sha1(b"blob %d\0" % len(data) + data).hexdigest()[:7]


changed_text = csv_text.replace(f"Tate Modern,{tate},", f"Tate Modern,{trial},")
text_holds(changed_text != csv_text, "the Tate Modern row of the data")
```

```{python}
#| label: first-show-file
#| include: false
def show_file(path: Path, lang: str = "markdown", lines: tuple[int, int] | None = None) -> str:
    """A file's text, as it is, or its lines first to last (counted from 1), in a fence longer
    than any run of backticks inside it."""
    text = path.read_text()
    if lines:
        text = "".join(text.splitlines(keepends=True)[lines[0] - 1:lines[1]])
    ticks = "`" * max(4, 1 + max(map(len, re.findall("`+", text)), default=0))
    return f"{ticks}{lang}\n{text}{ticks}"


# `cat report.qmd` is shown in three parts, split at its blank lines: the settings (lines
# 1-4), the cell (6-16) and the sentences (18-26). Stop if the starter changes.
qmd_lines = report.splitlines()
SETTINGS, CELL, SENTENCES = (1, 4), (6, 16), (18, len(qmd_lines))
text_holds(len(qmd_lines) == 26 and qmd_lines[3] == "---" and qmd_lines[4] == ""
           and qmd_lines[5] == "```{python}" and qmd_lines[15] == "```" and qmd_lines[16] == ""
           and qmd_lines[17].startswith("Five of London"),
           "the starter's report.qmd, split at its blank lines (lines 1-4, 6-16 and 18-26)")


def trimmed(hunks: list[str], keep: int = 1) -> list[str]:
    """Hunks as git_hunks gives them, with only `keep` unchanged lines on each side of a change
    (the @@ lines stay as Git prints them)."""
    changed = [i for i, line in enumerate(hunks) if line[:1] in "+-"]
    return [line for i, line in enumerate(hunks)
            if line.startswith("@@") or any(abs(i - j) <= keep for j in changed)]
```

Somewhere in this chapter's report is a wrong number. The report renders without a single
error, reads perfectly well and cites its source, and one of its figures is out by
`{python} f"{gap:,}"` visits. Finding it takes no programming, only a habit: put each number
beside the data it came from.

That habit is the *Check* in this book's title, and this chapter is where you practise it
with your own hands. You type every command yourself, at the terminal, on a real report:
copy it, render it, check it, record it with Git, change it and undo the change, break it
three ways on purpose and read the errors. Only at the end does the agent make an edit, and
you check its work with the same commands you have just learned. Allow about 45 minutes;
less if the terminal is already familiar.

::: opener
- Copy a project, move into it and render it from the terminal.
- Check every number in a report against its data, and trace a wrong one to where it was typed.
- Record, compare and undo changes with `git status`, `git diff`, `git restore` and `git commit`.
- Read an error from its first line, and check an agent's change before you commit it.

Start from
: the end of @sec-setup: the tools installed and `~/quarto-workshop` cloned in Step 5.

You build
: `~/first-report`, a one-page report whose every number matches its data, with a Git
  history of two commits.

Checkpoint
: none needed: the starter is the checkpoint. If you get lost, rename your copy with `mv`
  (*move*, which also renames), `mv ~/first-report ~/first-report-old`, and copy the starter
  again (@sec-first-files).
:::

## Get the files {#sec-first-files}

Step 5 of @sec-setup cloned the workshop's files into `~/quarto-workshop`. Among them is a
small report, `starters/first-report`. Copy it out, so that the original stays as it was.
Type it with **Tab completion**, which saves typing and catches mistakes: type
`cp -R ~/quarto-workshop/st` and press Tab, and the terminal finishes the name, `starters/`.
When several names fit, press Tab again to list them. When Tab does nothing at all, no name
starting that way exists there, which is worth knowing before you press Enter. In the
terminal, in any folder:

```bash
cp -R ~/quarto-workshop/starters/first-report ~/first-report
```

`cp` copies, and `-R` (*recursive*) copies a folder with everything inside it. It prints
nothing. Many commands work this way: `cp`, `cd` and, later, `git add` say nothing when they
succeed, and speak only when something is wrong. In the terminal, silence is success.

::: pitfall
If `cp` says `No such file or directory`, your copy of the workshop is older than this chapter:
`cd ~/quarto-workshop`, then `git pull`, then run the `cp` line again.
:::

Now move into the copy and look around. In the terminal:

```bash
cd ~/first-report
pwd
ls
```

`pwd` prints the folder you are in, ending in `first-report` (`/home/ana/first-report` on
Linux, `/Users/ana/first-report` on a Mac, with your own name). `ls` lists
`{python} n_files` names, in an order that depends on your system:

| Name | Holds |
|---|---|
| `report.qmd` | the report's source: settings, one code cell and its sentences |
| `data/` | `visits.csv`, the data the report reads |
| `AGENTS.md` | the project's rules for the agent (@sec-agents-md) |
| `README.md` | what the folder is, in a few lines |
| `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` | the Python packages the report needs, with exact versions |

: What the starter holds. {#tbl-first-files}

::: tryit
If you have not yet, copy the starter and go into it with `cd ~/first-report`.

::: done
`pwd` prints a path ending in `first-report`, and `ls` lists `report.qmd` and `data`.
:::
:::

The folders in this book have no spaces in their names; @sec-terminal's section on
[paths](../appendices/b-terminal.qmd#sec-keys-paths) shows what a space does.

## Render it yourself {#sec-first-render}

In the terminal, in `~/first-report`:

```bash
uv run quarto render report.qmd
```

`uv run` runs a command in the project's own Python environment (@sec-reproducible;
@sec-environments has more). The first time, it builds that environment from `uv.lock`, which
takes from a few seconds to a minute, and may print some `Downloading` lines first. Then
Quarto renders, and prints a good deal (trimmed here where marked …):

::: transcript
```text
Using CPython 3.12.13
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Installed 39 packages in 301ms

Starting python3 kernel...[IPKernelApp] WARNING | …
Done

Executing 'report.quarto_ipynb'
  Cell 1/1: ''...Done

pandoc
  to: html
  output-file: report.html
  …
Output created: report.html
```
:::

When a render succeeds, its last line is `Output created: report.html`. The lines after
`pandoc` are its settings, and the `IPKernelApp` warning is harmless
(@sec-step-test). Your Python version, package count and timings may differ.

Open the page. In the terminal, run `open report.html` (Mac), `xdg-open report.html`
(Linux), or `explorer.exe .` and then double-click `report.html` (Windows, in Ubuntu). The
browser shows:

> **Five London Sights**
>
> Five of London's best-known sights had `{python} f"{total:,}"` visits between them in
> 2025. The most visited was the `{python} top`, with `{python} f"{visits[top]:,}"`, and
> `{python} n_free` of the five are free to enter.
>
> Tate Modern, on the South Bank, had `{python} f"{planted:,}"` visits.
>
> Source: ALVA, "Visits made in 2025 to visitor attractions in membership with ALVA" (only
> ALVA member attractions are counted).

Now open the folder itself: `open .` (Mac), `xdg-open .` (Linux) or `explorer.exe .`
(Windows, in Ubuntu), where `.` means "this folder". The file browser shows the same files as `ls`,
plus the new ones the render made: `report.html` and `report_files/`. The terminal and the
file browser are two views of one folder.

::: tryit
Render the report and open `report.html`.

::: done
the render ends with `Output created: report.html`, and the page shows the five sights' total.
:::
:::

## Check every number against the data {#sec-first-check}

The render worked. That proves the code ran, not that the report is right. Look at the data.
In the terminal, in `~/first-report`:

```bash
cat data/visits.csv
```

`cat` prints a file. A CSV is a table in plain text, with commas between the columns. This
one has a first line naming its `{python} n_cols` columns, then `{python} n_rows` rows, one
for each sight. Each row carries its `source`, `url` and `retrieved` date, so the lines are
long and wrap. Ask for just the first two columns:

```bash
cut -d, -f1,2 data/visits.csv
```

`cut` keeps some columns of each line: `-d,` says the columns are separated by commas, and
`-f1,2` keeps the first and second. It splits at every comma, even one inside quotes, so it
is safe here only because the first two columns hold no commas.

::: transcript
```{python}
#| output: asis
screen([",".join(line.split(",")[:2]) for line in csv_lines])
```
:::

::: think
Put the page beside this list. Which of the page's numbers does not match a row? (The total
is the sum of the five; a calculator will confirm it, but you need not.)

Tate Modern's. The page says `{python} f"{planted:,}"`; its row says `{python} tate`: two
digits swapped. Nothing warned you, because Quarto rendered the sentence faithfully: to Quarto
it is just words. To fix it, find where that number came from.
:::

The report's source says where each number comes from. In the terminal:

```bash
cat report.qmd
```

It prints the whole file, shown here in three parts. First come the settings, between the
`---` lines:

::: transcript
```{python}
#| output: asis
print(show_file(START / "report.qmd", "text", SETTINGS))
```
:::

Then a code cell that reads `data/visits.csv` and computes `total`, `top` and `free`:

::: transcript
```{python}
#| output: asis
print(show_file(START / "report.qmd", "text", CELL))
```
:::

Then the sentences. The `` `{{python}} …` `` pieces are inline code, which Quarto replaces
with computed values:

::: transcript
```{python}
#| output: asis
print(show_file(START / "report.qmd", "text", SENTENCES))
```
:::

You met these parts in @sec-what-quarto, and @sec-compute explains every line. For now,
notice what is computed and what is not. Every other number on the page is inline code that
reads the data; the Tate Modern sentence was typed.

::: why
A typed number is a copy, made once by a person, and nothing connects it to the data
afterwards. Swapped digits are the classic copying slip, but the deeper problem is what
happens next: when the data change, the copy stays as it was. That is the drift of @sec-drift,
and @sec-first-change lets you watch it happen.
:::

::: tryit
Check the free count too: `cut -d, -f1,3 data/visits.csv` shows each sight's `admission`.

::: done
you have counted `{python} n_free` rows starting "Free", as the page says, and can name the
one number that is typed rather than computed.
:::
:::

## Start a history {#sec-first-git}

Before you change anything, record the report as it is, so that you can always get back to
it. Git, which you installed in @sec-setup, does this (@sec-reproducible). In the terminal,
in `~/first-report`:

```bash
git init -b main
```

::: transcript
```text
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/ana/first-report/.git/
```
:::

The folder is now a *repository*: it has a hidden `.git` folder where Git keeps the history.
`-b main` names the repository's first *branch*, its line of history, `main`, as GitHub does.
(This needs Git 2.28 or newer; `git --version` shows yours, and the setup in @sec-setup
installs a newer one.) Ask Git what it sees:

```bash
git status
```

::: transcript
```text
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	.gitignore
	AGENTS.md
	README.md
	data/
	pyproject.toml
	report.qmd
	uv.lock

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
```
:::

*Untracked* files are ones Git can see but does not yet record. Three things in the folder are
missing from the list: `.venv/`, `report.html` and `report_files/`. They are left out by
`.gitignore`, a file that lists what Git should ignore; `ls` hides it because its name starts
with a dot, and `ls -a` shows it. It names everything that `uv` and the render rebuild, so the
history holds only the sources.

Record everything else as the first *commit*, a saved state with a message saying why:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Starter report, as copied"
```

`git add .` prints nothing: it chooses what goes into the next commit, and `.` means "this
folder", everything not ignored. `git commit` records it:

::: transcript
```text
[main (root-commit) 15856fe] Starter report, as copied
 7 files changed, 916 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 …
```
:::

The seven characters after `root-commit` name the commit; yours will differ. Check again:

```bash
git status
git log --oneline
```

::: transcript
```text
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
15856fe (HEAD -> main) Starter report, as copied
```
:::

The *working tree* is the files in the folder as they are now; "clean" means they are exactly
as the last commit recorded them. `git log --oneline` lists the commits, newest first, and
`(HEAD -> main)` marks the commit your files are at now.

::: pitfall
If `git commit` says "Author identity unknown", run the two `git config --global` lines it
prints, with your own name and email (Step 5 of @sec-setup sets them), then commit again.
Without `-m "…"`, Git opens an editor for the message: leave it without saving (in nano,
Ctrl+X; in Vim, Esc, then `:q!` and Enter) and run the command again with `-m`.
:::

::: tryit
Start the history and make the first commit.

::: done
`git log --oneline` shows one commit, and `git status` says `working tree clean`.
:::
:::

## Predict, change, rebuild {#sec-first-change}

Suppose ALVA corrects Tate Modern's figure upwards by `{python} f"{BUMP:,}"`. Make that change
to the data yourself, with `nano`, the terminal's own small text editor. In the terminal, in
`~/first-report`:

```bash
nano data/visits.csv
```

Press the down arrow `{python} downs` times to reach the `Tate Modern` row; its long line runs
off the right edge of the window, which is fine. Press the right arrow until the cursor is just
after the first digit of `{python} code(tate)`, press Backspace to delete the
`{python} code(first_old)`, and type `{python} code(first_new)`, so that the number reads
`{python} code(trial)`. Save with Ctrl+O, then Enter; leave with Ctrl+X.

<!-- nano opening Pico: seen on macOS 26, 2026-11-12. -->

::: pitfall
In nano, Ctrl+O ("write Out") asks for the file name: press Enter to keep it. Ctrl+X leaves;
if you have not saved, nano asks first: Y then Enter saves, N throws the changes away. The
keys are listed along the bottom of the screen, where `^` means Ctrl. On a Mac, `nano` opens
Pico, which uses the same keys.
:::

Before you render, ask Git what you changed:

```bash
git status
git diff
```

If the diff is longer than the window, Git shows it a screen at a time, with `:` or `(END)` on
the last line: press Space for more and `q` to get your prompt back. Removed lines are red and
added lines green.

::: transcript
```text
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   data/visits.csv

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
```
:::

A *diff* is the lines a change removed and added. Here it is trimmed: the real lines are
long, so each is cut short where you see …, and only one unchanged line is kept on each side
of the change, without the `index` line Git prints second:

::: transcript
```{python}
#| output: asis
screen(["diff --git a/data/visits.csv b/data/visits.csv",
        "--- a/data/visits.csv", "+++ b/data/visits.csv"]
       + [line if line.startswith("@@") else short(line)
          for line in trimmed(git_hunks(csv_text.splitlines(), changed_text.splitlines()))])
```
:::

Read it from the top. `---` is the file before, `+++` after, and `@@ … @@` says which lines
follow. A line starting `-` was removed, a line starting `+` was added, and a line starting
with a space is unchanged context. One line changed, in one file: exactly the edit you meant.

::: think
Before you render: of the report's four numbers (the total, the most visited sight's count,
the free count and Tate Modern's), which will change?

Only the total, which rises by `{python} f"{BUMP:,}"` to `{python} f"{total_after:,}"`. The
`{python} top` is still the most visited, the free count is still `{python} n_free`, and the
Tate Modern sentence still says `{python} f"{planted:,}"`. It was typed, so it cannot follow
the data, not even when the data change in the very row it describes.
:::

Now rebuild and look. In the terminal:

```bash
uv run quarto render report.qmd
```

Reload `report.html` in the browser (it does not reload itself). The total now reads
`{python} f"{total_after:,}"`, and the Tate Modern sentence has not moved. That is
@sec-drift on your own screen: one input changed, the computed numbers followed it, and the
typed one was left behind.

The trial value is not real, so undo it:

```bash
git restore data/visits.csv
git status
```

::: transcript
```text
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```
:::

`git restore` puts a file back as it was at the last commit. It is the undo for any file Git
tracks, and it is final: the change it discards was never recorded, so it is gone. Render
once more, and the page is back to `{python} f"{total:,}"`.

::: tryit
Change the data, predict, render, compare, then restore and render again.

::: done
your prediction matched the page, and `git status` says `working tree clean`.
:::
:::

## Three mistakes on purpose {#sec-first-errors}

Errors are messages, not verdicts, and they are easiest to learn from when you caused them
on purpose. For each mistake below, make it, read the message, and check one piece of
evidence before you fix anything. Three rules for reading an error:

- **Find the first line that says `ERROR` or `error`**, often in red: it says what went wrong.
  When a long stack trace follows, scroll up to it.
- **Look where the caret `^` points**, when there is one: that is where the program noticed.
- **Skip the stack trace.** Many Quarto errors end with `Stack trace:` and a list of lines
  starting `at …`, eight for a wrong folder and more than twenty for broken settings. A *stack
  trace* lists what was running inside Quarto when it stopped: it is for Quarto's developers,
  not for you.

### The wrong folder {.unnumbered}

In the terminal:

```bash
cd ~
uv run quarto render report.qmd
```

::: transcript
```text
ERROR: No valid input files passed to render

Stack trace:
    at _Command.actionHandler (file:///…/quarto.js:142967:11)
    …
```
:::

::: think
Quarto found no file to render. Before you change anything, what do you check?

Where you are, and what is there: `pwd` prints your home folder, and `ls` shows no
`report.qmd`. The command was right and the folder was wrong. A misspelt name, such as
`reprot.qmd`, gives the same message, and `ls` shows that too. Fix it with `cd ~/first-report`,
then render again: the last line is `Output created: report.html`.
:::

### A typo in the command {.unnumbered}

In the terminal, in `~/first-report`:

```bash
uv run quatro render report.qmd
```

::: transcript
```text
error: Failed to spawn: `quatro`
  Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)
```
:::

::: think
What does the first line tell you, and what is the fix?

uv could not start a program called `quatro`, because there is none. The error quotes the
name back: compare it, letter by letter, with what you meant. Press the up arrow to bring the
command back, correct it, and press Enter. Without `uv run`, the shell says the same thing in
its own words: `zsh: command not found: quatro` on a Mac, `quatro: command not found` on
Ubuntu.
:::

### Broken settings {.unnumbered}

Open `report.qmd` with `nano report.qmd`, delete the space after the colon in `format: html`
so that it reads `format:html`, save and leave. Then, in the terminal:

```bash
uv run quarto render report.qmd
```

::: transcript
```text
ERROR: YAMLException: can not read a block mapping
entry; a multiline key may not be an implicit key (4:1)

 1 |
 2 | title: "Five London Sights"
 3 | format:html
 4 |
-----^

Stack trace:
    at …
```
:::

(The first line is one line on your screen, split here to fit; the stack trace runs to more
than twenty lines.)

::: think
The caret points at line 4, which is empty. Where is the mistake, and how do you check?

On line 3, the line above. `(4:1)` means line 4, column 1, counted inside the settings
block, where line 1 is the opening `---` and shows as empty. Without the space, `format:html`
is not a setting, so YAML, the format of those settings, reads on and gives up at line 4. Look
at the caret's line and the line above it. `git diff` shows the one line you changed.
:::

Fix it by putting the space back, or with the general undo, `git restore report.qmd`. Then
render again to confirm: the last line is `Output created: report.html`.

::: tryit
Make all three mistakes, read each message, check the evidence, then fix it.

::: done
the render ends with `Output created: report.html`, and `git status` says
`working tree clean`.
:::
:::

## Hand the fix to the agent {#sec-first-agent}

You know where the bug is, you can see any change with `git diff`, and you can undo one with
`git restore`. That is the moment to delegate: not before you can check the work, but as soon
as you can. Start your agent in the report's folder. In the terminal:

::: {.you}
```bash
cd ~/first-report
claude
```
:::

Type `codex`, `agy` or `opencode` in place of `claude` if that is your agent. Trust the folder when it
asks, because you made it (in Claude Code, press the down arrow first: the choice starts on No). (Codex asks here, and not in `~/setup`, because this folder is now a Git
repository.) Then, at the agent's prompt:

::: {.prompt}
```default
In report.qmd, the sentence about "Tate Modern" types its visit count by hand. Replace the typed number with inline code that reads Tate Modern's `visits_2025` from data/visits.csv. Do not change data/visits.csv. Render with `uv run quarto render report.qmd` and tell me the number the sentence now shows.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
reads `AGENTS.md`, `report.qmd` and `data/visits.csv` · edits `report.qmd` · `uv run quarto render report.qmd`
:::

::: {.you}
approve its commands · `/exit` · then, in the terminal, `git status` and `git diff`
:::

The starter's `AGENTS.md` already says that `data/visits.csv` must never be edited and that
every number comes from the data through inline code, so the agent is likely to get this
right. Likely is not checked.

::: think
The agent reports: "Done. The sentence now shows the figure from the data." Why run `git diff`
anyway?

The agent's message is a claim about the files; the diff shows the files themselves, every
file and line that changed, including any the agent did not mention, such as an edit to the
data.
:::

### Three checks for every change {#sec-three-checks}

Every change in this book, yours or the agent's, passes the same three checks: two before you
commit it, and one after. Here they are, applied to this one:

| Check | Asks | Here |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Did only the files I meant change? | `git status` lists `report.qmd` alone |
| Correctness | Does one number match its source row? | the page's Tate Modern figure against its row |
| Rebuild | Does what you committed build on its own? | a fresh clone renders (below) |

: The three checks, applied to the agent's first edit. {#tbl-three-checks}

**Scope.** `git status` should list one modified file, `report.qmd`. If `data/visits.csv` is
listed too, the agent broke the project's rule: `git restore data/visits.csv` undoes that
part. The diff will look something like the two parts below, from a version written by hand
to test the step; an agent's will differ in detail. It is trimmed: the `diff --git` and
`index` lines are left out, and one unchanged line is kept on each side of a change. The
first change adds two lines to the cell:

```{python}
#| include: false
# The tested hand-made fix, applied to the starter's own report.qmd, as Git's two hunks.
src = report.splitlines()
i_free = next(i for i, line in enumerate(src) if line.startswith("free = "))
fixed = (src[:i_free + 1]
         + ['tate = next(int(r["visits_2025"]) for r in rows',
            '            if r["attraction"] == "Tate Modern")']
         + src[i_free + 1:])
fixed = [line.replace(typed.group(0),
                      'Tate Modern, on the South Bank, had `{python} f"{tate:,}"` visits.')
         for line in fixed]
text_holds(fixed != src, "the hand-made fix to report.qmd")
fix_lines = [line if line[:1] in "+-" else short(line, 44) for line in trimmed(git_hunks(src, fixed))]
at = [i for i, line in enumerate(fix_lines) if line.startswith("@@")]
text_holds(len(at) == 2, "the fix's two hunks: the cell, then the sentence")
cell_hunk, sentence_hunk = fix_lines[at[0]:at[1]], fix_lines[at[1]:]
text_holds(sum(l.startswith("+") for l in cell_hunk) == 2 and not any(l.startswith("-") for l in cell_hunk),
           "the first hunk adds the cell's two lines")
```

::: transcript
```{python}
#| output: asis
screen(["--- a/report.qmd", "+++ b/report.qmd"] + cell_hunk)
```
:::

The second replaces the typed number with inline code that looks Tate Modern up in the data:

::: transcript
```{python}
#| output: asis
screen(sentence_hunk)
```
:::

**Correctness.** Reload `report.html`: the sentence should now say
`{python} f"{tate:,}"`, which is `{python} tate` in the `Tate Modern` row of the `cut` output
in @sec-first-check.

If either check fails, `git restore report.qmd` puts the file back as it was before the agent
touched it, and you can ask again. Undo works on the agent's changes exactly as on yours.

When both pass, commit, in the terminal:

```bash
git commit -am "Compute Tate Modern's visits from the data"
git log --oneline
```

`-a` adds every tracked file that changed, so you need no `git add`; `-m` gives the message.
Your hash, and perhaps the count of lines, will differ:

::: transcript
```text
[main d7e7f02] Compute Tate Modern's visits from the data
 1 file changed, 3 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
d7e7f02 (HEAD -> main) Compute Tate Modern's visits from the data
15856fe Starter report, as copied
```
:::

**Rebuild.** The last check asks whether everything the report needs is in the history, and
not only in your folder. Clone the repository into `/tmp`, a folder for temporary files, which
the computer empties from time to time, and render the clone. In the terminal:

```bash
git clone ~/first-report /tmp/first-report-check
cd /tmp/first-report-check
uv run quarto render report.qmd
```

::: transcript
```text
Cloning into '/tmp/first-report-check'...
done.
```
:::

The clone has no `.venv/` and no `report.html`, because `.gitignore` kept them out of the
history, so the render prints `Creating virtual environment` again and then builds the page.
(If Git says the destination already exists, you have run this before: pick another name,
such as `/tmp/first-report-check2`.) Open the clone's page as you opened yours:
`open report.html` (Mac), `xdg-open report.html` (Linux), or `explorer.exe .` and then
double-click `report.html` (Windows, in Ubuntu). It should match yours,
`{python} f"{tate:,}"` and all. If the clone does not render, something the report needs was
never committed: add it and commit again. Then `cd ~/first-report` to go back; the clone is
disposable.

::: tryit
Run the prompt, check its diff, commit, and rebuild from a fresh clone.

::: done
`git log --oneline` shows two commits, and the clone's page says Tate Modern had
`{python} f"{tate:,}"` visits.
:::
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- A report that renders without an error can still be wrong: put each number beside its row
  in the data, and trace a wrong one to where it was typed.
- Typed numbers drift and computed ones follow the data. Change one input, predict, rebuild
  and explain.
- `git status` says what changed, `git diff` shows how, `git restore` undoes it and `git commit`
  records a state you can return to.
- Read an error from its first line and the caret, skip the stack trace, and check one piece of
  evidence (`pwd`, `ls`, `git diff`) before you fix anything.
- Delegate a change once you can check it: scope, correctness and rebuild (@tbl-three-checks),
  then commit.
:::

You have now made, by hand, every check the rest of the book asks you to make of an agent's
work, on a project small enough to see whole. Part II scales it up. Each project starts as this one did, with
`git init`, so every agent edit in it can be seen with `git diff` and undone with
`git restore`. @sec-markdown starts the London guide from an empty folder and explains, one
construct at a time, the Markdown you have just been reading.
